section.title: Melchizedek
section.sectionRationale: This chapter is a single connected episode: a war of kings, Lot's capture, Abram's daring rescue, and the meeting with the mysterious priest-king Melchizedek. It belongs together because the whole narrative builds to that encounter, where Abram is blessed by God Most High and refuses the spoils of Sodom.
section.thesis: Abram routs a coalition of kings to rescue Lot, then meets Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, whose blessing and bread and wine lift the story from war to worship and point ahead to a greater priest-king, Jesus.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the war of the nine kings and Lot's capture; Abram's rescue with his household; the blessing of Melchizedek and Abram's tithe; and Abram's refusal of the king of Sodom's reward.

units.label: The war of the kings
units.note: Lot swept up in Sodom's fall

verses.text: In those days Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim
went to war against Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar).
The latter five came as allies to the Valley of Siddim (that is, the Salt Sea).
For twelve years they had been subject to Chedorlaomer, but in the thirteenth year they rebelled.
In the fourteenth year, Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him went out and defeated the Rephaites in Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzites in Ham, the Emites in Shaveh-kiriathaim,
and the Horites in the area of Mount Seir, as far as El-paran, which is near the desert.
Then they turned back to invade En-mishpat (that is, Kadesh), and they conquered the whole territory of the Amalekites, as well as the Amorites who lived in Hazazon-tamar.
Then the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar) marched out and arrayed themselves for battle in the Valley of Siddim
against Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goiim, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar, four kings against five.
Now the Valley of Siddim was full of tar pits, and as the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, some men fell into the pits, but the survivors fled to the hill country.
The four kings seized all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah and all their food, and they went on their way.
They also carried off Abram’s nephew Lot and his possessions, since Lot was living in Sodom.
Then an escapee came and reported this to Abram the Hebrew. Now Abram was living near the Oaks of Mamre the Amorite, a brother of Eshcol and Aner, all of whom were bound by treaty to Abram.
And when Abram heard that his relative had been captured, he mobilized the 318 trained men born in his household, and they set out in pursuit as far as Dan.
During the night, Abram divided his forces and routed Chedorlaomer’s army, pursuing them as far as Hobah, north of Damascus.
He retrieved all the goods, as well as his relative Lot and his possessions, together with the women and the rest of the people.
After Abram returned from defeating Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him, the king of Sodom went out to meet him in the Valley of Shaveh (that is, the King’s Valley).
Then {{melchizedek|Melchizedek}} king of Salem brought out bread and wine, since he was {{kohen|priest}} of {{el-elyon|God Most High}},
and he blessed Abram and said: “Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth,
and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.” Then Abram gave Melchizedek {{maaser|a tenth}} of everything.

units.label: Abram and the king of Sodom

verses.text: The king of Sodom said to Abram, “Give me the people, but take the goods for yourself.”
But Abram replied to the king of Sodom, “I have raised my hand to the LORD God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth,
that I will not accept even a thread, or a strap of a sandal, or anything that belongs to you, lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’
I will accept nothing but what my men have eaten and the share for the men who went with me, Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre. They may take their portion.”

melchizedek.gloss: The name means king of righteousness, and as king of Salem he is also king of peace. He appears without recorded genealogy, both priest and king, which is why Psalm 110 and Hebrews 7 take him as a type of Christ, a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.

kohen.gloss: A priest, one who mediates between God and people. This is the first time the word appears in the Bible, and strikingly it names not an Israelite but a Canaanite king who worships the true God, a priesthood older than Levi that foreshadows the everlasting priesthood of Jesus.

el-elyon.gloss: God Most High, the sovereign Creator of heaven and earth. Melchizedek worships Him, and Abram identifies this Most High God with the LORD, Yahweh, in verse 22, confessing that the God of the covenant is the one supreme God over all kings and nations.

maaser.gloss: A tenth, a tithe. Abram gives a tenth of the spoils to Melchizedek, an act Hebrews 7 uses to argue that Melchizedek's priesthood, and so Christ's, is greater than Levi's, since Levi in a sense tithed through Abram to Melchizedek.

basic.context: Four powerful kings sweep through the region and defeat the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah, carrying off loot and captives, including Abram's nephew Lot. Abram hears of it, gathers 318 men from his household, and rescues Lot in a daring night raid. On his way home he meets a mysterious priest-king named Melchizedek.
basic.hermeneutics: The key question is who Melchizedek is and why he matters so much. He is king of Salem and priest of God Most High, and he blesses Abram with bread and wine. The rest of the Bible treats him as a picture of Christ, a priest and king who serves the true God.
basic.originalLanguages: Melchizedek means king of righteousness, and Salem means peace, so he is king of righteousness and peace. He is the first priest, kohen, named in the Bible, and he serves God Most High, El Elyon, the Creator of heaven and earth. Abram gives him a tithe, a tenth of everything.
basic.typology: Melchizedek is one of the clearest pictures of Jesus in the Old Testament. He is both king and priest, he brings out bread and wine, and he has no recorded beginning or end. Psalm 110 and Hebrews say Jesus is a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek, greater than the priests of Israel.
basic.christ: Jesus is the true King of righteousness and Prince of peace, and He is our great High Priest, not from the line of Levi but in the order of Melchizedek. The bread and wine Melchizedek brings out point ahead to the Lord's Supper. In Jesus, kingship and priesthood come together forever.
basic.god: God is God Most High, the Creator of heaven and earth, sovereign over every king and army in the story. He gives Abram the victory, and He is worshipped by Melchizedek. He is the God who provides, so that Abram can refuse Sodom's riches and trust Him alone.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 110 calls the coming King a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. Hebrews 7 unfolds this at length. And the bread and wine anticipate the meal Jesus gives His people.
basic.oneStory: In a chapter of war and plunder, a priest-king suddenly appears, blesses Abram, and lifts the story to worship. Melchizedek is a signpost to Jesus, the King and Priest who blesses His people and gives them bread and wine, and Abram's refusal of Sodom shows the faith that trusts God Most High rather than the world's rewards.

context.literary:
Genesis 14 reads unlike anything around it. The chapters on either side are intimate family stories; this one opens like a royal chronicle, with a date formula, 'In those days,' a roster of nine kings and a campaign itinerary. Its style is terse and old fashioned, and it keeps stopping to update ancient place names for later readers: Bela 'that is, Zoar,' the Valley of Siddim 'that is, the Salt Sea,' En-mishpat 'that is, Kadesh,' the Valley of Shaveh 'that is, the King's Valley,' verses 2, 3, 7 and 17.

The chapter moves in four stages. Verses 1 to 12 give the war, and the whole international drama narrows to its last line: Lot was carried off, 'since Lot was living in Sodom.' Verses 13 to 16 give the rescue. Verses 17 to 24 give two meetings with two kings.

That last section is carefully built. The king of Sodom 'went out to meet' Abram in verse 17, but before he can say a word, Melchizedek steps into the story in verses 18 to 20. Only in verse 21 does Sodom's king finally speak. The priest-king's blessing is set inside the other king's approach, so the reader hears Melchizedek's words first and can measure Sodom's offer against them. Melchizedek brings out bread and wine and gives a blessing; the king of Sodom brings nothing and bargains. Melchizedek receives a tenth; the king of Sodom is refused even a thread.

The chapter also carries forward the key word of Genesis 12:2-3, bless. Melchizedek says 'blessed' twice, once of Abram and once of God, and Abram's refusal of Sodom's wealth shows that he will be made rich only by the One who blesses. The chapter answers Genesis 13 as well. Lot chose the plain for its wealth, and the plain's wealth is exactly what the invaders carry off, with Lot among it.
context.historical:
The invading kings come from the far east of the known world. Shinar is Babylonia, as the BSB notes; Elam lay east of the Tigris in what is now southwestern Iran; Ellasar and Goiim, 'nations,' are harder to place. Chedorlaomer, who leads, has a name with an Elamite ring. An older generation of scholars identified Amraphel with Hammurabi of Babylon, but that link has been widely abandoned, and none of the four kings has been securely matched with a known ruler. What the text does reflect is a real pattern of the early second millennium, when eastern powers could extract tribute from distant regions and punish rebellion by force.

The route runs down the east side of the Jordan through the territories of peoples Deuteronomy later remembers as giants, the Rephaim, Zuzites and Emites, Deuteronomy 2:10-11 and 3:11, then around the south to Kadesh and back up to Hazazon-tamar, which 2 Chronicles 20:2 identifies as En-gedi on the Dead Sea. This is broadly the line of the later King's Highway, Numbers 20:17. The tar pits of verse 10 fit the Dead Sea basin, long known for its bitumen.

Abram's force of 318 men 'born in his household' shows that he was a substantial chief with trained dependants, and his alliance with Mamre, Eshcol and Aner, verse 13, uses the Hebrew for a covenant, as the BSB footnote explains. He pursues as far as Dan in the far north, a name the city bore only later, Judges 18:29, another sign that the text was updated for Israelite readers, and on past Damascus.

Salem is almost certainly Jerusalem; Psalm 76:2 sets Salem in parallel with Zion. Jerusalem kings later bore names formed like Melchizedek's, such as Adoni-zedek in Joshua 10:1, and the King's Valley lay near the city, 2 Samuel 18:18. God Most High, El Elyon, was a known title for a supreme deity in the region, and Abram's oath in verse 22 claims it for the LORD alone. Raising the hand was a gesture of oath, Deuteronomy 32:40 and Daniel 12:7.
context.canonical:
Within Genesis the chapter explains why Lot needed rescuing and prepares for the next. Lot is saved here by Abram's sword and in Genesis 19 by Abram's prayer, and both times he is living in Sodom. The words of Melchizedek's blessing, 'who has delivered your enemies into your hand,' introduce the word God uses of Himself in the next verse of Genesis, 'I am your shield,' Genesis 15:1, as the note on the Hebrew explains. The tithe returns when Jacob vows a tenth at Bethel, Genesis 28:22, and becomes law for supporting the Levites, Numbers 18:21.

Melchizedek disappears from the story for a thousand years and then surfaces in a single line of Psalm 110. The psalm addresses David's Lord, who sits at God's right hand and rules from Zion, and adds the oath, 'The LORD has sworn and will not change His mind: You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek,' Psalm 110:4. A king from Zion who is also a priest, not by Levi's line but by a divine oath, could only be modelled on the one priest-king of Salem that Scripture knew. Zechariah 6:13 looks for the same union, the Branch who 'will be a priest on His throne.'

The New Testament builds on both texts. Jesus applies Psalm 110:1 to Himself, and Hebrews quotes verse 4 again and again, Hebrews 5:6, 5:10 and 6:20. Hebrews 7 then reads Genesis 14 closely: the meaning of Melchizedek's name and city, the silence about his ancestry, the tithe from Abraham, and the principle that 'the lesser is blessed by the greater,' Hebrews 7:7. The argument is that a priesthood older and greater than Levi's has always existed in Scripture, and that Jesus holds it 'by the power of an indestructible life,' Hebrews 7:16.

The title God Most High also runs through the canon, in the Psalms, Psalm 47:2, in Daniel, Daniel 4:34, and even on the lips of demons, 'Jesus, Son of the Most High God,' Mark 5:7.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to see their father as more than a wandering herdsman. The man who let Lot choose the best land in Genesis 13 is no weakling. When his kinsman is captured he acts at once, at risk to himself, against the kings who had just crushed five local rulers and a string of warlike peoples. The first hearers were to see that faith is not passivity; it moves to rescue.

The author also meant them to see where Abram's victory came from. Melchizedek interprets the battle before Abram says a word about it: God Most High 'delivered your enemies into your hand.' The credit goes up, not to Abram's tactics.

Most of all, Moses shows Abram choosing between two sources of wealth and security. The king of Sodom offers goods as the price of a deal. The king of Salem offers bread, wine and blessing in the name of the Creator. Abram gives a tenth to the one and refuses even a sandal strap from the other, so that no one could say, 'I have made Abram rich,' verse 23. Israel, surrounded by kings who would offer alliances and wealth, was to learn that the promise of Genesis 12:2 would be kept by God, and that accepting riches from corrupt powers would compromise the witness that God alone blesses.

Finally, by identifying God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth, with the LORD in verse 22, the chapter teaches that Israel's covenant God is not one local deity among many but the Maker and Owner of everything.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records a war, a rescue, a tithe and an oath, and none of these is directly commanded here. Abram's military action is described, not offered as a model for private warfare; it concerns the rescue of captives and involves allies bound by treaty. Abram's refusal of spoil is also his own vow, and he explicitly allows his allies to take their share, verse 24. He does not make his conscience a rule for others.

The tithe to Melchizedek is voluntary and precedes the law. Christians have long debated whether it establishes a lasting principle of giving; at the least it shows that honouring God with a portion of what He gives is older than Sinai. What carries forward most clearly is the disposition the chapter commends: courage in helping others, giving credit to God for every victory, generosity toward God's servants, and a refusal to let one's security rest on gifts from those who oppose God, Hebrews 13:5.

debates.question: Who is Melchizedek?

views.label: A historical Canaanite priest-king who is a type of Christ
views.case: Genesis presents him as a real king of a real city, Salem, serving God Most High. Hebrews 7:3 says he was 'like the Son of God,' which compares him to the Son rather than identifying him with the Son. The silence about his parents is a feature of how Scripture presents him, and Hebrews builds its argument on that silence. This has been the majority view in the church.

views.label: A preincarnate appearance of the Son of God
views.case: Some read 'without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life,' Hebrews 7:3, as a literal description that no mere human could satisfy, and conclude that this was Christ Himself appearing to Abram.

views.label: Shem or another known figure
views.case: An old Jewish tradition identified Melchizedek with Shem, who by the chronology of Genesis 11 could still have been alive. The text never makes this link, and it would undercut Hebrews' point that his ancestry is unrecorded.

debates.bearing: Hebrews says he 'remains a priest for all time' as one 'like the Son of God,' which is the language of likeness, not identity. Reading him as a real man whom Scripture deliberately presents without origins lets the type do its work: he points to a greater Priest whose life truly has no end.

debates.question: Does Abram's tithe set a binding pattern for believers?

views.label: Yes, the tithe is a principle that predates and outlasts the law
views.case: Abram tithes before Moses, Jacob vows a tenth before Moses, Genesis 28:22, and Hebrews 7 treats Abram's tithe as honouring a priesthood that continues in Christ. On this view a tenth remains a fitting standard for Christian giving.

views.label: No, it is a free act of honour, not a rule
views.case: Genesis records the tithe once, from war spoil, without command. The New Testament never requires a tenth of believers, and speaks instead of generous, willing, proportionate giving, 2 Corinthians 9:7. Hebrews uses the tithe to prove Melchizedek's greatness, not to legislate.

debates.bearing: The passage shows that honouring God with a portion of His gifts is older than the law and fitting for those He has blessed. Whether a tenth is required or simply a wise starting point, the heart of it is Abram's: he gives because he has been given the victory.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 13 calls him 'Abram the Hebrew,' ivri, the first time the word appears in the Bible. Genesis 10:21 has already named Eber as an ancestor of Shem's line, and the word most naturally means a descendant of Eber. It may also carry the sense of one from across, from the root avar, to cross over, fitting a man who came from beyond the Euphrates. In Genesis it is usually a label outsiders use of Israelites, as it is here in a chapter written like a foreign chronicle.

The 318 are chanikhim, 'trained men.' The root chanakh means to dedicate or initiate; it gives the noun for the dedication of the altar, Numbers 7:10, and the verb in 'Train up a child,' Proverbs 22:6. These are men raised and prepared in Abram's own household.

Melchizedek's title for God in verse 19 is qoneh shamayim va'arets, 'Creator of heaven and earth.' The verb qanah most often means to acquire or buy, as with property, but in a few places it clearly means to make or bring forth: Eve says 'I have brought forth a man,' Genesis 4:1, and Moses asks, 'Is He not your Father and Creator?' Deuteronomy 32:6, and in Proverbs 8:22 the BSB renders it 'The LORD created me.' The title therefore holds both ideas together. God made heaven and earth and so owns them. That is the point Abram presses in verse 22 when he takes the title on his own lips.

The blessing turns on a wordplay that links this chapter to the next. 'Who has delivered your enemies' uses miggen, from a verb meaning to hand over or deliver up. It shares its consonants with magen, shield, the word God uses in Genesis 15:1, 'I am your shield.' The God who has just handed Abram's enemies to him will be Abram's protection from their revenge.

Melchizedek is called a kohen, the standard Old Testament word for priest and its first appearance in Scripture. His blessing uses baruk twice, blessed be Abram and blessed be God, the same word that framed Abram's call in Genesis 12:2-3. The act of blessing moves both ways, from God to man through the priest, and from man back to God in praise.

The tenth is ma'aser, from the ordinary word for ten. Abram's oath in verse 22 is literally 'I have lifted my hand,' and verse 23 uses a strong negative idiom, 'if from a thread to a sandal strap,' an oath formula whose unstated ending is something like 'may God deal with me.' Abram binds himself before God not to take the smallest scrap from Sodom.

typology.type: Melchizedek, king of righteousness and king of Salem
typology.fulfillment: Hebrews 7:2 draws out the name and city: 'king of righteousness' and 'king of peace.' Christ is both in reality. The child of Isaiah 9:6-7 is 'Prince of Peace' who reigns 'with justice and righteousness,' and through Him believers are justified and have 'peace with God,' Romans 5:1. Melchizedek's righteousness and peace were titles over a small city; Christ's are the substance of a kingdom without end. The type falls short in that Melchizedek's rule was local and temporary, while Christ reigns forever, Isaiah 9:7.

typology.type: A priest with no recorded beginning or end
typology.fulfillment: Genesis gives Melchizedek no parents, no birth and no death, and Hebrews 7:3 reads that silence as a portrait: he 'remains a priest for all time.' Psalm 110:4 swears that the coming King will be 'a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek,' and Hebrews says Jesus became a priest 'by the power of an indestructible life,' Hebrews 7:16, and 'always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:25. What was a literary silence in Melchizedek is a literal truth in Christ, whose priesthood truly never ends.

typology.type: The priest-king who blesses Abram and receives his tithe
typology.fulfillment: Hebrews argues that 'the lesser is blessed by the greater,' Hebrews 7:7, and that Levi, still in Abraham's loins, paid the tenth through him, Hebrews 7:9-10. Melchizedek's priesthood thus outranks Aaron's. Christ holds this higher order, so that the Levitical priesthood was never the final word, Hebrews 7:11. In Israel king and priest were kept apart, but Zechariah 6:13 foresaw one who 'will be a priest on His throne,' and Jesus unites both offices in Himself.

typology.type: The bread and wine brought out to the victor
typology.fulfillment: Melchizedek brings bread and wine to Abram after battle, a gift of refreshment and fellowship. Hebrews does not mention the bread and wine, so the link to the Lord's Supper is an echo rather than a stated type, but a natural one. Jesus took bread and the cup and gave them as His body and 'blood of the covenant,' Matthew 26:26-28, and promises that His people will 'eat and drink at My table in My kingdom,' Luke 22:30. Melchizedek fed a weary warrior; Christ feeds His people with His own life.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the psalm that interprets it. Psalm 110 speaks of a King enthroned at God's right hand, and then of an oath: 'You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek,' Psalm 110:4. Jesus identified Himself as the Lord of that psalm, Matthew 22:43-45, and Hebrews applies its fourth verse to Him repeatedly, Hebrews 5:6, 5:10 and 6:20. The priest-king of Genesis 14 is the pattern for the Messiah's own office.

It leads to Christ by the union of offices. In Israel, king and priest were separate; Uzziah was struck with leprosy for burning incense in the temple, 2 Chronicles 26:18-19. Melchizedek held both, and so does Christ. He rules as King and intercedes as Priest, 'holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners, and exalted above the heavens,' Hebrews 7:26.

It leads to Christ by the greatness of this priesthood. Hebrews 7 reasons from details in Genesis 14: Abraham, who held the promises, gave the tithe and received the blessing, so Melchizedek is greater than Abraham, and therefore greater than Levi who descends from him. If perfection had come through the Levitical priests, Hebrews asks, why would God later swear an oath about a priest 'in the order of Melchizedek and not in the order of Aaron'? Hebrews 7:11. Christ's priesthood does not rest on genealogy but on an oath and an indestructible life, Hebrews 7:16 and 7:20-21.

It leads to Christ by the shape of the scene. A priest-king comes out to a weary victor with bread and wine and a blessing from God Most High. Christ comes to His people with bread and cup, Matthew 26:26-28, and with a blessing that rests on His own finished work. And where Abram refused to be enriched by the king of Sodom, Christ refused the kingdoms of the world from the tempter, Matthew 4:8-10, trusting the Father to give Him the nations.

Care is needed. Hebrews does not build on every detail, and it never mentions the bread and wine. Nor does it say Melchizedek was Christ; it says he was 'like the Son of God.' The type works because Scripture itself presents him as a figure without origins, whose priesthood is matched and surpassed by the Son who truly has neither beginning nor end.
study.god:
The chapter's central disclosure is a name: El Elyon, God Most High, qoneh shamayim va'arets, Creator and Owner of heaven and earth. It appears four times in five verses. Around it swirls a war of nine kings, with coalitions, rebellions and plunder, and the title quietly puts all of them in their place. However high Chedorlaomer rises, there is One higher. Deuteronomy 32:8 uses the same title for the God who 'gave the nations their inheritance' and set their boundaries. The kings of Genesis 14 are moving pieces on a board that belongs to Him.

God's sovereignty is shown in how the victory is interpreted. Abram fought, planned and divided his forces at night, but Melchizedek's verdict is that God Most High 'delivered your enemies into your hand.' Human effort and divine action are not rivals here. God works through Abram's courage without making Abram the source of the victory.

God's universality is shown in who worships Him. Melchizedek is not from Abram's family and is never said to have received a call like Abram's, yet he is 'priest of God Most High.' Knowledge of the true God is not confined to one household. And when Abram says, 'I have raised my hand to the LORD God Most High,' verse 22, he claims that the God of the covenant is the very God whom Melchizedek serves, the Maker of all.

God is also shown as the true source of wealth. Because He owns heaven and earth, Abram does not need Sodom's goods. His refusal is theology in action: to take the king of Sodom's gift would be to let Sodom share credit for what God had promised to give, Genesis 12:2. Proverbs 30:8-9 prays for the same kind of dependence.

For worship, the chapter gives a pattern: blessing God for His deliverance, 'blessed be God Most High,' giving Him a portion of what He has given, and refusing any source of security that would rival Him. Psalm 121:2 puts the same confession in a pilgrim's mouth: 'My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.'

crossReferences.note: The only Old Testament mention of Melchizedek outside Genesis. God swears that David's Lord, the King enthroned at His right hand, is 'a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.' The psalm takes the priest-king of Salem as the pattern for the Messiah, uniting throne and priesthood in one Person.

Hebrews reads Genesis 14:18-20 line by line: the meaning of Melchizedek's name and city, the silence about his ancestry, and the tithe. Since the lesser is blessed by the greater, and Levi paid the tenth through Abraham, Melchizedek's priesthood is shown to be greater than Levi's.

The decisive contrast: Christ is a priest 'not by a law of succession, but by the power of an indestructible life.' The feature that marked Melchizedek in Genesis, a priest with no recorded genealogy, becomes in Christ a priesthood grounded in resurrection life.

'His tent is in Salem, His dwelling place in Zion.' The psalm sets Salem in parallel with Zion, supporting the identification of Melchizedek's city with Jerusalem, the city where God would later place His name and where the true Priest-King would die and rise.

The Branch will build the LORD's temple, sit on His throne and rule, 'and He will be a priest on His throne.' The union of kingship and priesthood first seen in Melchizedek becomes a prophetic hope for the Messiah, fulfilled in Jesus.

Immediately after refusing Sodom's goods, Abram hears, 'Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your very great reward.' The word shield echoes Melchizedek's 'delivered' in 14:20, and the promised reward answers the reward Abram refused. God replaces what Abram gave up.

Jacob vows, 'of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth.' Like Abram's tithe in 14:20, it comes before the law and responds to God's provision. The tithe in Genesis is a grateful acknowledgement that everything comes from the God who gives.

Elisha refuses Naaman's gifts: 'I will not accept it.' Like Abram refusing the king of Sodom in 14:22-23, the prophet will not let a foreign ruler think he has purchased God's favour or made God's servant rich. The refusal protects the glory of God's free gift.

Jesus takes bread and the cup and gives them as His body and blood of the covenant. The bread and wine Melchizedek brought out in Genesis 14:18 are not explained in Hebrews, but the priest-king offering bread and wine to God's servant finds a deep echo in Christ's supper.

The Levitical priests were many because death cut each one short, but Jesus 'lives forever' and 'always lives to intercede.' The priest who met Abram once and blessed him points to the Priest who never stops blessing and praying for His people.

A man possessed by demons cries out, 'Jesus, Son of the Most High God.' The title first spoken by Melchizedek, God Most High, is attached to Jesus, and even the powers of evil acknowledge His authority over them.

'My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.' The pilgrim's confession gathers up the title of Genesis 14:19 and 22, the Creator of heaven and earth, and makes it the ground of trust for every traveller, as it was for Abram when he refused Sodom's wealth.

study.oneStory:
The story so far has been full of kings who reach for power. Nimrod built his kingdom in Shinar, Genesis 10:10, and Babel's builders in Shinar reached for the heavens, Genesis 11:2-4. In Genesis 14 a king of Shinar marches again, with allies, to subdue and plunder. The world after Eden is a world of empires that take.

Into that world God has called Abram with a promise of blessing, Genesis 12:2-3. Chapter 14 shows the promise at work in a violent setting. The man who will not grasp for land in chapter 13 will fight to free a captive in chapter 14, and when the fighting is over he will not grasp for plunder either. Then a priest-king appears, and the key word of Abram's call, blessed, is spoken over him in the name of God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth. For a moment the reader sees what a true king looks like: one who feeds, blesses and serves God, rather than one who takes.

The chapter sets up a thread that runs a thousand years forward. Salem becomes Jerusalem, where David reigns and Solomon builds the temple. Yet Israel's kings could not be priests, and its priests could not be kings, and both offices failed. Psalm 110 then speaks of a coming King who would also be 'a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek,' reviving the ancient pattern.

That hope is fulfilled in Jesus, who rules at God's right hand and intercedes as Priest, Hebrews 7:25. He is the King of righteousness and peace in fact, and He has made His people 'a kingdom, priests to His God and Father,' Revelation 1:6, and 'a royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9.

The story ends in a city. Salem, the city of peace, gives way to the new Jerusalem, where the redeemed reign with Christ and serve God. Every king who took will be gone, and the Priest-King who gave Himself will bless His people forever at His table.

quiz.q: Why did Abram set out with 318 men?

options.text: To rescue his nephew Lot, who had been captured by the four kings.
options.note: Abram acted to save his kinsman swept up in Sodom's defeat.

options.text: To conquer Sodom and take its throne for himself.
options.note: Abram sought to rescue Lot, not to seize a kingdom.

options.text: To plunder the retreating kings for their wealth.
options.note: He later refuses the spoils; his aim was rescue, not plunder.

options.text: To defend his household and allies from attack.
options.note: There is a protective element, but the clear purpose was to rescue Lot.

quiz.q: Who is Melchizedek in this chapter?

options.text: King of Salem and priest of God Most High who blesses Abram.
options.note: He is both king and priest and serves the true God.

options.text: The king of Sodom offering Abram a reward.
options.note: That is a different king; Melchizedek offers blessing, not spoils.

options.text: One of the four invading kings from the east.
options.note: He is not among the warring kings; he is the priest-king of Salem.

options.text: A mysterious priest-king the Bible later links to Christ.
options.note: True and important, though the passage first identifies him as king of Salem and priest of God Most High.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament use Melchizedek?

options.text: As a type of Christ, a priest forever whose order is greater than Levi's.
options.note: Psalm 110 and Hebrews 7 present Jesus as a priest in Melchizedek's order.

options.text: As an example of a bad king to avoid.
options.note: He is honoured, not condemned; he blesses Abram and points to Christ.

options.text: As the founder of the Levitical priesthood.
options.note: His priesthood is older than and distinct from Levi's.

options.text: As a picture of Jesus who unites king and priest.
options.note: True and central, though the fuller point is the superiority of his priestly order.

quiz.q: Why did Abram refuse the king of Sodom's goods?

options.text: So no one could say Sodom, not God Most High, had made him rich.
options.note: Abram trusted God as his provider rather than a doomed king's reward.

options.text: Because the goods were too heavy to carry home.
options.note: His reason was faith and reputation, not the weight of the loot.

options.text: Because he had already taken enough plunder secretly.
options.note: Abram took nothing for himself; the refusal was principled.

options.text: To keep his trust and security in the LORD alone.
options.note: True and close to the heart, expressed in his concern that God, not Sodom, be his enricher.

quiz.q: What do the bread and wine of Melchizedek point toward?

options.text: The Lord's Supper that Christ, our priest-king, gives His people.
options.note: The bread and wine foreshadow the meal Jesus institutes.

options.text: A bribe to win Abram's loyalty.
options.note: They are part of a priestly blessing, not a bribe.

options.text: Ordinary provisions with no deeper meaning.
options.note: In context and in Hebrews they carry rich significance.

options.text: A sign of fellowship and blessing from God Most High.
options.note: True at one level, and ultimately they anticipate Christ's supper.

questions: Abram risked everything to rescue Lot, the relative who had chosen the best land for himself. Who is God calling you to help, even someone who once wronged or overlooked you?
After the battle, Melchizedek lifted Abram's eyes from war to worship. What practices help you return to worship after stressful or draining seasons?
Abram refused Sodom's wealth so his security would rest in God alone. Where are you tempted to let the world, rather than God, be the source of your confidence?
Jesus is our King and Priest forever, always alive to bless and intercede for us. How does it steady you to know you have a priest-king praying for you right now?
Melchizedek's bread and wine point to the Lord's Supper. How might coming to that table with fresh eyes deepen your trust in Christ this week?

translationNotes.note: God Most High renders the Hebrew El Elyon; Abram in verse 22 joins this title to the covenant name, the LORD, confessing that Melchizedek's Most High God is the same God who called him.

A tenth of everything is the first tithe in Scripture; Hebrews 7 builds on it to argue that Melchizedek's priesthood, and therefore Christ's, is greater than the Levitical priesthood descended from Abram.
